articles.title: Carrie Ending Explained: Who Lived, Who Died, and What Could Mike Flanagan Have in Mind Next for This Universe?
articles.summary: Mike Flanagan's Carrie has arrived on Prime Video. So who lived, who died, and what could be next in this universe?
articles.body:
Full spoilers for Prime Video’s Carrie Season 1 follow.

From the moment Mike Flanagan revealed that his version of Carrie would involve multiple young women with telekinesis, not just the title character, there was some scoffing from people asking why Flanagan was interjecting some sort of an X-Men element into this well-told story. But those who asked this have likely either never read Stephen King’s original 1974 novel upon which the series is based or don’t recall its details, because as Flanagan himself has noted, this wasn’t something he was inventing out of whole cloth — it’s an idea plucked straight from the source material itself.

Carrie was the first King book ever published, and it laid a lot of groundwork for what was to come in his later stories. First and foremost, it was a freaky horror tale that involved a whole lot of people being killed by the end. But also of significance is that the book’s protagonist — and ultimately the cause of all that death — is a human girl who also happens to have amazing mental powers she was born with, something King explicitly stated was not unique to Carrie. In the book, he noted there were in fact others out there with powers like hers, and in his later works — which mostly take place in an interconnected universe — he introduced many such characters.

Flanagan's new series gives Carrie a major overhaul by not just moving the story to the present day but also reinterpreting Carrie, her mother Margaret, and other important characters in the story. Flanagan has also interwoven a plot line about other women with telekinetic powers becoming aware of Carrie and seeking her out. And oh yeah… Carrie lives at the end!

Unlike in King’s book and almost all of the other adaptations to date, rather than die in the aftermath of the massacre she set in motion, Carrie (Summer H. Howell) is instead able to escape town with the help of one of those aforementioned fellow telekinetic girls (and to be fair, one other adaptation also had Carrie survive; the 2002 TV-movie written by Bryan Fuller).

This lays the groundwork for potential future seasons of Carrie, as Flanagan does a ton of world-building through the series that’s inspired by King’s larger body of work. Read on for more about how Carrie Season 1 ended, the ways it intersected with the Stephen King universe and its other examples of people with amazing mental powers, and where it could go next.

Generally speaking, things played out in the finale as they usually do in a Carrie adaptation, starting with the cruel “prank” played on Carrie at prom involving pigs’ blood being dumped on her by Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton) and her boyfriend Billy Nolan (Arthur Conti). The fragile, bullied Carrie, who’d thought she’d finally been accepted, lashes out, and an outright massacre occurs thanks to Carrie’s telekinesis, which takes out most of the prom attendees and then others as Carrie makes her way through the streets of Chamberlain, Maine.

But one major change here is the inclusion of the character Emaline (Thalia Dudek), another telekinetic, who was speaking to Carrie from afar all season through her mind. When Carrie uses her powers to try to yank down Chris and Billy from the rafters, her mental deflection of the landing that falls toward her ends up inadvertently hitting and killing her date, Tommy Ross (Joel Oulette). This is a deviation from the book, in which one of the metal buckets holding the blood hits Tommy in the head, making Chris and Billy the only ones responsible for his demise.

Here, however, Carrie is distraught about Tommy and agrees when Emaline appears and asks if she can “take the wheel” from Carrie, meaning that the lion’s share of the 200+ deaths that occur that night are with Emaline controlling Carrie’s body, albeit with Carrie allowing it to happen. It’s merciless mayhem to be sure, taking out good-hearted characters like Principal Grayle (Matthew Lillard) — who’s electrocuted while standing on stage — and Rita “Miss D” Desjardin (Amber Midthunder). Rita’s death is extra tragic because she’s running to help Carrie as Amanda (Katee Sackhoff), someone who’s come to the prom expressly to kill Carrie because she knew she had powers thanks to Carrie’s mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan), is trying to shoot her. But Carrie/Emaline instinctively gives Miss D a telekinetic swat as she runs up to Carrie, sending her flying into the burning stage to her doom. Grayle and Miss D have also been killed at the prom in other adaptations, though it should be noted that King himself allowed these characters to survive, albeit suffering from understandable misery and PTSD from what occurred.

Those who do survive include Carrie’s classmates, Sue Snell (Siena Agudong) and Tina Blake (Josie Totah), who are among the few to make it out of the school gymnasium alive before the doors are telekinetically locked and the floor is electrocuted. Both Sue and Tina are among those later interrogated in the aftermath by the mysterious Adelaide (Flanagan’s wife and frequent collaborator, Kate Siegel). Also surviving are some non-students who were at the prom — young women with telekinesis (Cassandra Naud and Flanagan regular Ruth Codd) who report to Adelaide and are smart enough to avoid Carrie’s deadly actions. As for Amanda, the last we see of her, she’s telekinetically shoved back onto a table, so there’s a bit of wiggle room there since we don’t explicitly see her death.

As for Chris and Billy, they escape the prom, but their later encounter with Carrie on the road ends in a variation of how it’s gone for them in King’s novel and in every other adaptation; she kills them inside their car. Notably too, we see it is definitely Carrie in control at this point, as Emaline stands to the side while Carrie flips Billy's car and crushes it with her powers, killing the two people whose actions most directly caused this misery to begin.

Then there’s Margaret, who attempts to kill her own daughter in King’s book as well as every previous adaptation, only to be killed herself by Carrie’s powers. Similar to the famous 1976 Brian De Palma Carrie film, Flanagan has Carrie’s powers cause the White family house to collapse, but unlike that film, where both women die , Carrie and Margaret both survive . In fact, Margaret reveals she has telekinetic powers herself, as she briefly holds up part of the house that was falling on her.

In the wake of all this, Carrie leaves with Emaline, but while Margaret survives this encounter, her life ends soon after regardless. While speaking to Adelaide, Margaret reveals this was only the second time she ever tapped into her telekinetic abilities, and she doesn’t think she can do it again. Now feeling Margaret is of no use to her, Adelaide causes Margaret’s heart to stop beating in the same way that Carrie killed her mother in the book.

If you’re a Stephen King fan looking for those connected universe moments that are prevalent throughout his books, it’s hard not to mark out when Adelaide tells Margaret, “A lot of people have a little bit of Shine and they don’t even know it,” The word Shine, of course, refers to the Shining — not just the story itself, but the term that gives that King classic (and its acclaimed Stanley Kubrick film adaptation) its title, which was how Overlook Hotel cook Dick Hallorann described those like himself and Danny Torrance who have psychic abilities.

The Shining/Shine has since been used as a catch-all term for all sorts of mental powers seen throughout King’s work, with fans long assuming it could retroactively be used for Carrie as well. Now, Adelaide gives that assumption on-screen confirmation when she uses it in relation to Margaret’s own telekinetic abilities. It’s also worth noting that Flanagan introduces the idea of Margaret herself having limited telekinetic powers, but in the book, it does run in the family, as Margaret’s grandmother was telekinetic.

While King says in the original Carrie that those with telekinesis specifically tend to be women, there are many other mental abilities and forms of the Shining seen throughout his stories that are possessed by both men and women. That includes the Shining itself and Doctor Sleep’s Danny Torrance’s ability to see and interact with the dead; the pyrokinesis of Firestarter’s Charlie McGee; and the clairvoyance of The Dead Zone’s Johnny Smith. King’s multipart epic, The Dark Tower, would also involve characters with the Shining, but there he uses another term for it — The Touch.

Though Amazon Prime has not yet made a decision on whether they’re renewing the series or not, Flanagan has said that he has a three-season plan for Carrie. Now that we’ve seen the end of Season 1, the road is quite literally wide open for Carrie White, as she heads toward a future we’ve never seen depicted before. Could that future include other familiar faces and elements from Stephen King lore? Certainly Flanagan would likely love that, but it’s important to note that the screen rights to King’s work has been spread out across so many studios through the years that many tantalizing possibilities are legally impossible… or at least quite tricky to sort out.

For instance, in Flanagan’s own adaptation of King’s Doctor Sleep, young Abra Stone — who has the Shining — is told by Danny Torrance that there are others out there that may need her help. Abra finding Carrie in her time of need would be a natural and exciting team-up, and Flanagan could even bring back Kyliegh Curran as Abra, but Warner Bros. made both the Doctor Sleep movie and its predecessor, The Shining, and likely still has the movie and TV rights to those characters.

Another young girl with incredible powers who it would be intrinsically fun to see Carrie meet up with is the Firestarter herself, Charlie McGee. But if Universal (who made both film versions of Firestarter) still holds the rights, that would be a similar problem. So while King has a vast amount of characters he’s created, some of which Carrie producer Amazon MGM may already have access to or be able to more easily get access to, there’s also a chance Flanagan will simply use concepts from King’s work and put his own spin on it, or introduce something that can easily co-exist alongside what’s already out there.

In fact, he seems to be doing just that with Adelaide and the telekinetic girls she’s gathering. King’s 2019 novel, The Institute, is about a place that’s similarly gathering children with mental abilities, though in a notably exploitative “let’s imprison them and turn them into weapons” manner. The woman running this program, Julia Sigsby, is somewhat reminiscent of Adelaide, except Sigsby has no powers of her own; she’s coldly abusive and using these kids without any apparent personal investment. Adelaide is certainly cutthroat — look at how she kills Margaret once she learns Margeret can’t access her abilities again — but also could be more of a Magneto type who justifies her actions as a greater good for her kind. Amusingly, The Institute has its very own TV show adaptation running right now, with Season 2 debuting soon.

Besides the direct mention of “Shine,” Carrie’s first season didn't lean into many direct references to King’s other work, though both LaMerk Industries and Sombra Corporation — companies with ties to key Dark Tower figures, The Man in Black and the Crimson King — were glimpsed in the series. Flanagan is actually developing a new Dark Tower project, but has admitted it’s been a tricky one to get off the ground. It remains to be seen if Carrie could be a direct tie to what he has planned there, or if — being the King superfan that he is — he simply included the references as easter eggs, reinforcing the ties all of this has to King’s larger universe.

Another route Flanagan could go in a second season would be to explore more aspects of the Carrie novel itself via material no one has ever tackled. The book has a loose time-jumping structure with elements of a true crime story, complete with excerpts from interviews, testimony, and books from the aftermath of the “Black Prom” in Chamberlain. Some adaptations have lightly nodded to this by using a framing device where characters are being interviewed about what happened, which Flanagan does himself with Adelaide. But the book hints at some massive nationwide fallout and coverage of the Black Prom, which makes sense considering a telekinetic teenage girl essentially destroyed a town. This includes mentions of the White Commission, a federal investigation into Carrie and what she did.

Introducing the White Commission is an enticing potential element for a future season of Carrie, especially because Carrie is now on the run. Beyond Adelaide’s group wanting to recruit her and those like Amanda wanting to find and kill her, you could have a government agency on her tail as well. Could this lead to something akin to The Institute, or could the story go in a whole other direction? There are a lot of possibilities.

We’ll have to wait and see if Amazon decides to renew Carrie before we have any chance of finding out exactly what her next step will be.

articles.title: GTA 6: The Big Interview
articles.summary: The in-depth interview with Rockstar North's Rob Nelson in full, as he played through 30 minutes of the game ahead of the Netflix reveal.
articles.body:
In July this year, IGN was invited to Rockstar North to see GTA 6 being played for the very first time, with Head of Development and Co-Studio Head Rob Nelson on the controller. It was honestly one of the most exhilerating experiences of my life – seeing GTA 6 in action before anyone else! And, when the Netflix extended look dropped in August, I was finally able to share my thoughts on what I'd seen . My preview detailed everything I saw in the exclusive 30-minute demo, which included a new-look wanted system , a new way to steal cars , and how Jason and Lucia's romantic relationship – although front-and-center in the demo and the Netflix video – is entirely optional.

I also spoke at length with Rob Nelson. He talked us through some of the big ideas in the game, the changes to some of the game mechanics we all know and love, and the 13-year development process that has gone into making Grand Theft Auto 6 the biggest, most immersive entry into the GTA series yet. The highlights of that conversation were published back in August too, but the entirety of that conversation has been sitting on my laptop... until now.

So why publish it, and why now? Although the coverage IGN ran back in August covers all the headline topics, the full interview captures what it was like to be in the room while GTA 6 was being played. It wasn't a prescribed demo and often things didn't work out as planned, and I found looking back over the full transcript of the interview really fascinating. And that's why I wanted to share the full interview with you, because I hope you find it fascinating too. As for the 'why now' of it all, why not now? It's GTA 6 and frankly I'm as excited for this game as anyone.

Since the interview took place while playing GTA 6, the conversation sometimes jumps around and often describes what’s happening on-screen, but I've done my best to fill in the gaps so you get a sense of what it was like. I hope you enjoy reading it as much as I loved watching it!

IGN: Obviously there are the set pieces and the story missions in GTA 6, but it seems there's a lot more for Jason and Lucia to do in the world…

Rob Nelson: There is a ton of stuff the player can do in GTA 6, as Jason and Lucia on their own or together, in between missions and story-driven content.

IGN: I'm also fascinated to know more about the couple dynamics…

Rob Nelson: We can just run the game and start walking around, I think that's the most natural way to do it.

The challenge for us on this game is the same as it is on any new game for us, which is – how do we evolve and build upon the good things we have done before, in all the ways these things need to evolve, but at the same time ensure that the game still has everything that made the previous games in this series resonate with people?

[The demo starts with Jason and Lucia hanging out at a Safehouse. Jason has longer hair than we saw in the trailer, and is busy grabbing a drink from the fridge, examining a romance novel he finds on a table, and interacting with Lucia.]

This is one of their Safehouses. Jason and Lucia can exist in this space together. This represents an exciting challenge for us: putting Jason and Lucia on schedules that feel believable and making the Safehouse a lot more interactive. The Safehouses [in GTA 6] are probably closer to the camps in RDR2 than they are to safehouses in any GTA game before, in terms of how interactive they are and how much they feel like your home. But this is not their own house, they’re staying in someone else’s house.

You can switch characters and pop over to the couch. We tried to keep this mechanic as open as possible, although there will obviously be times during the narrative where it's not possible.

We have some basic cosmetic options in the Safehouse where you can adjust minor things and do some simple stuff to your hair—cut it shorter or shave it off. In the Safehouse, it’s only reductive – if you want new hairstyles you have to go to a hair salon or barber. There are a lot of hair salons and clothing shops all over the world and each place has some standard stuff you can get, and then also stuff that is unique to those places to really encourage exploration.

For now, I'm going to go out on my own for a little while and have a look around…

[Nelson takes Lucia on a stroll around downtown on her own, wandering through an urban park packed with people talking, a man walking his dog on a leash, joggers, and everything you'd expect to see in any busy city.]

One of the coolest things about this game being developed from the ground up on this generation of hardware is taking advantage of all the memory that we have on the latest generation of consoles, combined with our teams’ experience doing this for so long together. NPCs have more height differentiation and body shape differentiation than ever before; we could never have had this variety before because different body types had to share animation sets. So if you had the same animation on the 5’6” person and the 6' 2" person, they wouldn’t line up if they're fighting or sitting in cars—basically, any interactions with each other or the environment. But [in GTA 6], the team worked out a system where they now retarget those animations on the fly. Now we have a huge variety of heights and shapes, and it all works together because of what this team was able to pull off.

The NPC interaction system is one that is returning and evolved from Red Dead Redemption 2. In the past we’ve had systems where you can speak to NPCs. In RDR1 and GTA 5 there were basic systems for interacting, but the interactions were very simple. But with Red Dead Redemption 2, we were finally able to incorporate the ability to interact with NPCs as a more fleshed-out system. Traditionally, L2 was a binary action that immediately aimed your gun at someone or locked onto them for combat. But as the resolution has increased, the experiences we create have had to evolve alongside that – the fidelity of them, how you can exist in them, and what you can do in them.

So on RDR2 we came up with a control solution where, if your gun is in your holster and you hold L2 to lock on to an NPC, you just have the option to talk to them. You can greet them or antagonize them, or you can pull R2 to draw your weapon. But adding those options into RDR2 created a huge challenge for us.

We have to do so much work in design, in code behaviors, in animation, and in writing to get these interactions to feel believable. Now, everybody across all of these teams – across technical teams, animation teams, across design teams, across writing teams – needed to, in a way, become students of human behavior. You find yourself watching how people behave out in the world and studying the rise and fall of a conversation as you pass two people. As you listen, you can count like 7 to 10 words and glean what they're talking about. To try and recreate the feeling of this properly, we ended up needing to build an entirely new team of writers, directors, and producers in LA to create the depth and breadth and variety of crazy people saying crazy things that we needed.

While we pushed this sort of interaction with NPCs as far as we could for Red Dead Redemption 2, with GTA 6 we are taking it much further. The team has done an incredible job to create all of this crazy dialogue, and you can stand there and listen to them, but we’ve tried to find a balance where if you stand too close to a group, they should notice you and notice that you're eavesdropping. So, if you stand there and try to listen to the whole thing, they'll often turn around, notice you and go, ‘Oh hey, can I help you?’ Or if you follow people for too long and too close so that they can hear you, they’ll go, ‘Oh, hey.’ Then they may be aggressive, or they may just want to get away from you. When we first started these ideas back on Red Dead Redemption 2, we thought if we could get it working in a more sparsely populated world, we imagined what it might feel like at scale in a modern world. So it was one of the scary but very worthwhile and fun challenges we took on with this game.

The world will act upon you as well as you acting upon the world. I think in previous GTA games you were a bit all-powerful. You were the only one with an invisible arsenal hidden away. Apart from the police, everyone would run in terror from you if you started acting out. This world in GTA 6 is not like that.

A huge amount of time and research and work went into populating the world, styling the people so that every district and every town that you go to feels appropriate. Hopefully for people who want it, it’s fun to just do this sort of open-world stuff, wander around, talk to people, explore, and see what happens.

[Nelson interacts with some NPCs when another group spots the interaction and pulls a gun.]

Rob Nelson: That escalated, yeah, they got involved – but nobody's dead. They're all still fine. They will get up and walk away. But somebody's called this incident in. Our dispatch is extremely specific in what it knows. This team has done an incredible job with this. If I get out of here, that’s a one-star Wanted level, which is not really a big deal. I aimed the gun at the person, which defused the situation, and they all ran. Otherwise, I would’ve ended up beating people up. If I get out of this area where the police are going to respond, I should be totally fine.

As much as possible, we tried to design the game so that you have options. Things can escalate quite quickly if you want them to, or people who don’t want to escalate can try to avoid it. It's not always possible! To me, that supports the narrative. This is a story about a couple on the run. We have tried to make the systems and the design support our narrative when and wherever possible. Meaning, if you hit and run, commit a crime and run, get into trouble and move on before the cops get there, and you don’t start shooting people, don't start escalating – which you absolutely can do if you want to – but if you don’t, you’re generally going to be fine.

So I can check my map – this is a hot area. The cops are there. If I go back, they'll be hanging around for a little while. You can see if I hover back over that area of the map, I still have one star in that area.

We have put some layers of stratification into the vehicles. Previously, you could just press triangle to automatically hotwire and steal any vehicle that you wanted and take off. We felt like that left a lot of potential gameplay on the table in terms of progression and decision-making for players. I think it gives all the vehicles more meaning, and you need to pay attention to what you’re doing a bit more. So now, you start off the game and there are certain parked cars that are not accessible to you until you get a bit further along with the story and you acquire certain tools to get into them, but you can always carjack any driver you see.

We also now have this scanner as a part of the phone, where you can put it over the vehicle and learn about it. For example, it tells me this car is locked, it's got an alarm, and has no tracker. It also tells me how much it’s worth if I go to take it to a Pay n’ Spray or a specialty car fence and how much it would cost for me to register it for myself.

So, for example, this car needs a key cloner. This other car will just need a slim-jim. So we’ve added a lot of fun little tools you need or mechanics you need to perform these formerly binary

Now, we can go and sell this truck, but it's not really worth very much. Is there anything you're interested in seeing?

IGN: I mean all of it! [Laughs] But some of those day-to-day things that you can go and do… that's one of my favorite things about Red Dead Redemption 2.

IGN: I finished Red Dead 2 a number of times and I had a save of it where I could just load it up and play.

Rob Nelson: That’s essentially what GTA 6 has as well – you can just exist.

[Nelson takes Lucia into one of the salons dotted around the map.]

Every one of these salons – and there’s many of them – has signature hairstyles. They also have the standard ones.

Similar to Red Dead Redemption 2, we put a lot of focus towards trying to make it so that you can do these sorts of open-world things in a very natural way.

IGN: I noticed that when you are doing things, sometimes there are little icons to say you did a good thing or a bad thing. Is there a reputation system?

Rob Nelson: There is a system that tracks what sort of criminal you are. And then there is also a relationship system. They're separate. You manage the relationship in the way you hopefully nurture any relationship – which is by spending time together. So being in the open world and exploring together or doing activities together – playing pool or mini golf or kayaking; normal slice of life things. Or robbing stores together, robbing banks together. However players want to spend that time together, it will have a positive impact on the relationship.

The reputation system you are asking about is something we call your Criminal Profile. It's different than the honor system in Red Dead Redemption 2. There isn’t a right or wrong way to play this game, but consistent sorts of actions may have an impact in terms of how the world reacts to you and how the narrative plays out.

In GTA 6, you are playing as criminals on the run but the narrative is such that it makes most sense for them to do what they need to do while not drawing unnecessary attention, even though sometimes that happens! So if you're doing things on a mission that you are required to do – or you’re robbing places, or somebody comes and messes with you and you have to deal with them by smacking them down or whatever – that’s all fair game. It's when you go beyond what is necessary on a consistent basis or you do completely unnecessary stuff consistently that you may start to sway your criminal profile in a certain direction. Maybe you care about that as a player, maybe you don't. There is no right or wrong way to play this.

To us, it's a very interesting concept. In previous games you’re quite overpowered in the world compared to everyone else apart from the cops, which can be fun but not as fun, I don’t think, as having a world where there may be other people that have impulses of their own and act upon you. You are still powerful and capable, but you are not the only one capable of violence or the only one with weapons or the only crazy person out there. It makes the world far more unpredictable and interesting. It's something that we started doing in Red Dead Redemption 2, where you are not the only dangerous person in the world. There are gangs that will attack you, things that will happen to you. The world will act upon you. That happens here a lot, and then when it does, you have a decision to make. How do you want to deal with it?

[Lucia is in another altercation with an NPC]

Rob Nelson: I hope they’re ready for it. I hope they like what we are trying to do with it.

IGN: I think they’ll be excited. And I think as well that one thing everyone will agree on is how exciting and deep the world is.

Rob Nelson: Yeah, how deep the world is can’t be denied. The team has done an incredible job pulling that together and making it feel consistent. That has been and continues to be an exciting challenge. We aren't quite there yet, and we will take every moment we can get to polish things!

IGN: I did a poll [on IGN], and we asked what our readers were really excited to know more about, and they were obsessed with the world. Almost 50% said the world. They really are excited to get in there and discover things.

Rob Nelson: Well, you’ve only seen a tiny, tiny slice of it in the city. I didn’t even get to the beach – you just can’t get to it all. But hey, that leaves some stuff for you to discover.

IGN: They’re cultural moments, the GTAs.

Rob Nelson: No pressure. [Laughs] I try not to think about it. You’re aware of it, of course. But I think we just have to try and make something that we feel is innovating on what we’ve done previously, evolving it while still making it feel familiar.

IGN: I like that the little bits of satire are in there, but it feels a little more heartfelt maybe than they have in the past.

Rob Nelson: That’s a question a lot of people ask: how do you deal with satire in today’s world? I think there's always stuff to satirize. As long as humans are humans, other humans will figure out ways to satirize what we do. For us, because we work on such a long development cycle, we have to not jump on stuff and instead choose our angle of approach carefully and decide what things are going to be a bit more timeless. We’re not a TV show coming out every week or every month. We have to be careful that what we’re choosing to satirize is not going to feel dated in a weird way.

I think those broader things are OK to satirize, but very specific political issues or memes will date fast. Even the way our characters speak, we think about it a lot so that they're not using extremely contemporary slang. Even though our characters are a certain age, they need to feel somewhat timeless.

IGN: I think as well, anything like slang, it immediately cuts out a large age demographic.

Rob Nelson: Exactly, exactly. Jason and Lucia as characters have rich backstories that we sometimes explicitly talk about and sometimes just allude to. I think there is enough detail there if you want to pay attention, but we also have purposely left them with some room for interpretation so that hopefully the connection can be enhanced between the player and these characters. That is maybe as important as it has ever been for these characters in particular because I think for this story to work for you, for you to buy into this relationship, you have to be able to connect with them in some way. Hopefully a good number of people will feel like they can do that.

IGN: Some people have grown up with GTA as kind of a cultural reference point, but this will be the first one they’ll have been around for the release of it.

Rob Nelson: Yeah, that’s crazy to think of – wow. For sure.

IGN: It seems similar to Red Dead Redemption 2 – people are going to be discovering things in this game for a really long time.

Rob Nelson: I hope so. There’s plenty in there.

IGN: People are going to have a lot of reactions to the trailer.

IGN: They’re going to be going through it with a fine-tooth comb…

Rob Nelson: [Laughs] Yes, I know. We’re trying our best to make it as clean as possible.

IGN: Is that a crazy thing? Knowing that because it’s you guys, every frame is going to be…

Rob Nelson: It’s a hard thing. As much pressure as we feel externally, I don’t think it can compare to the pressure we put on ourselves as a team. Everyone wants things to be perfect. We are nervous! Nervous, of course, but also excited to see how people respond to this video and then ultimately the game. It is definitely a step forward in all respects for us – the size of the world and how deep it feels. It’s a bit of a shock when you get in there and you see the density of the traffic, the density of population, and the fidelity of their responses to you.

IGN: I went back and fired up GTA 5 just to go back in there, and yeah, seeing this, it’s wild, the difference. Because I remember being like, 'Oh, that was so manic and the world was so full.’ And it was, but not like this.

Rob Nelson: Yeah, I think with RDR2, we finally had the team and the tech and then took the time we needed to push the idea of making a fully realized consistent-feeling world further than we ever had. With that game we took the time necessary to take advantage of that generation of hardware to maximize the quality of our open-world population, design, and gameplay so that when you were riding from here to there in-game, you were constantly getting distracted and pulled in different directions. And then you could really get lost as that character in that place.

That's when, to me, these games can feel magical and create a sense of wonder that the world is alive – and you get these little shivers of ‘What’s happening?’ GTA 6 is a continuation of our team pushing in this direction – doing everything we possibly can to create the largest, deepest, most densely populated and complex world we have ever built for people to get lost in.

IGN: It’s one of the things I loved in Red Dead Redemption 2, but you also have a lot of open space in that game.

Rob Nelson: Yes, the density of GTA 6 has been an exciting challenge, but that's also part of the reason why our team has doubled in size.

IGN: Anything else you wanted to talk about?

Rob Nelson: I just really wanted to show that in addition to what we hope will be a very compelling story for people to get involved in, there is a very deep, vast, incredible world to explore and get involved with as these two characters – apart, or together – however you want to play it. And finally, even though there are some new systems at play, it's still very much Grand Theft Auto.

Rachel Weber is the Head of Editorial Development at IGN and an elder millennial. She's been a professional nerd since 2006 when she got her start on Official PlayStation Magazine in the UK, and has since worked for GamesIndustry.Biz, Rolling Stone and GamesRadar. She loves horror, horror movies, horror games, Red Dead Redemption 2, and her Love and Deepspace boyfriends.

articles.title: Scream’s 30th Anniversary Collector’s Set Includes a Bloody Cordless Phone
articles.summary: The '90s horror classic Scream is getting a 30th anniversary collector's set that includes the movie in 4K along with detective case files and a bloody cordless phone.
articles.body:
Hard to believe it’s been 30 years since Wes Craven’s horror classic Scream hit theaters. To celebrate, Paramount is releasing Scream 30th Anniversary Collector’s Set, an Amazon-exclusive bundle that includes the movie along with a number of physical items. Preorders are live now ( see it at Amazon ). It costs $119.99 and is set to release on December 15.

Scream: 30th Anniversary Collector's Set

This collector’s set comes with the movie on 4K UHD, Blu-ray, and digital. It also includes case file items of the kind a detective would compile. But the pièce de résistance is a replica of the cordless phone made famous during the opening scene in which Ghostface calls Drew Barrymore’s character to terrify her before moving in for the kill. The phone has blood stains on it, and plays “iconic quotes.”

By 1996, the slasher movie had become a somewhat played-out genre. We’d gotten nine Friday the 13th movies, seven Nightmares on Elm Street, and six Halloweens. Horror fans basically knew what to expect from them, even including the order in which the characters would die.

Pretty much instantly upon release, Scream breathed (stabbed?) new life into the genre by adding a meta layer in which the characters in the movie knew the horror movie tropes. It also featured a likable cast of characters played by Neve Campbell, David Arquette, Courteney Cox, Matthew Lillard, Rose McGowan, Skeet Ulrich, and Drew Barrymore. Combine that with the ongoing mystery of who Ghostface is as the bodies pile up, and you have a thrilling new entry in the genre.

Scream would go on to spawn numerous sequels of its own , some of which are better than others (Scream 2 still rules, btw). But the original movie boldly carved itself into the horror canon, becoming a staple of the genre and one of the best horror movies of the ‘90s.

articles.title: Superhero Satire The Wrong Earth Takes on Absolute Batman in Absolutely the Wrong Earth - NYCC 2026
articles.summary: AHOY Comics revealed an impressive lineup of new books at NYCC, including the Absolute Batman parody Absolutely the Wrong Earth.
articles.body:
NYCC 2026 kicks off today, and AHOY Comics is one of many publishers taking to the show to reveal what's in store for 2027. Among AHOY's new offerings is the latest entry in the popular superhero satire series The Wrong Earth. This time around, it's Absolute Batman's turn to be parodied in a new one-shot special dubbed Absolutely the Wrong Earth.

IGN can exclusively reveal all four new AHOY Comics titles being showcased at NYCC. Read on to learn more about each one.

Indie comics publisher AHOY Comics’s first-ever title—THE WRONG EARTH by writer Tom Peyer (Hourman) and award-winning artist Jamal Igle (creator of Molly Danger and artist of Dudley Datson and the Forever Machine)—blew the multiverse concept wide open with two parallel heroes inhabiting different worlds: Earth-Alpha’s bright and campy Dragonflyman and Earth-Omega’s dark and gritty Dragonfly. The fan-favorite satire kicked off a series of acclaimed titles featuring Dragonfly, Dragonflyman, and their kid sidekick(s) Stinger, including DRAGONFLY VS. DRAGONFLYMAN, THE WRONG EARTH: NIGHT & DAY, THE WRONG EARTH one-shots, THE WRONG EARTH: WE COULD BE HEROES, and THE WRONG EARTH: DEAD RINGERS. Now prepare to meet the final version of your favorite superhero on the wrongest earth in Peyer and Igle’s latest can’t-miss collaboration: ABSOLUTELY THE WRONG EARTH, a hilarious and action-packed oversized 40-page one-shot which rappels into stores near you on April 7.

This January, writer Mark Russell (X-Factor, Second Coming) and artist Mauricet (Howl) – the team behind indie publisher AHOY Comics’s innovative one-shot Thanksgiving, which IGN called “hilarious but disturbingly relevant” – will reunite for a brand-new chilling tale in KINDERGARTEN GULAG, a disturbing meditation on the innocent things that can hurt us most. The darkly funny one-shot follows Igby, a man who wakes up to find himself the sole inmate in a prison run by five very young, very creepy children arguing about whether or not to kill him. KINDERGARTEN GULAG will land in stores on January 27, 2027.

Creative Team: Eric Palicki & Chris Peterson

Something strange is happening in Chicago, starting with the gruesome murders of the Suydam family. Enter Paul Corduroy, a P.I. and monster killer who handles cases the police can’t—and who’s about to learn a few shocking things about himself, too. Writer Eric Palicki, creator of Atlantis Wasn’t Built for Tourists and Black’s Myth, and artist Chris Peterson (Grindhouse) presents a brutal mix of mystery and paranormal action in the tradition of Hack/Slash and Something Is Killing the Children.

Creative Team: Eric Palicki & Giulia Lalli

Somewhere in the Pacific Northwest on an ill-fate camping trip, Ashleigh Cole stumbles upon a dying dragon in the woods, its hide peppered with bullet wounds and tattooed with U.S. military markings. Ash returns to her mundane life, convinced her experience in the woods was all just a hallucination—until she begins to display some oddly dragonlike characteristics herself. Compelled by voices in her mind, Ash undertakes a mission to rescue other captive dragons and help the mythical creatures escape—but the shadowy government organization determined to turn them into weapons of mass destruction has other plans. Funny, heartfelt, and action-packed, DRAGONPROOF will appeal to adult readers who grew up on Buffy and Gargoyles and capture the imagination of post-YA readers of The Fourth Wing, ACOTAR, and more. DRAGONPROOF is funding soon on Kickstarter.

You can preorder these upcoming titles at your local comic shop .

Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky .
